quote: The word “consciousness,” if it has any meaning at all, refers to that-which-is or that-which-causes or that-which-makes-me-say-I-have inward awareness.
content: This premise is the whole argument, and it is the point in dispute. Fixing the reference of “consciousness” by its causal role, as whatever makes one report awareness, is analytic functionalism (Lewis (1972)), the position that Chalmers’s first two chapters argue against on the ground that the concept of experience is not a functional concept: one can grasp the concept fully and still ask whether the thing playing the role is experienced. Once premise (4) is granted, the conclusion that zombies are contradictory follows in one line, which is why the essay can present the “proof” so briskly and why the philosophers who reject the premise are unmoved by it. The essay’s Twin Earth analogy, on which the Zombie World lacks consciousness as Twin Earth lacks H2O, is the Kripkean a posteriori necessity move, and Kripke argued, in the third of the lectures that introduced the move, that it fails for exactly this case (Naming and Necessity, 1980, pp. 144–155): for water there is a gap between how it appears and what it is, so an appearance-duplicate could be XYZ, but for pain the appearance is the thing, so there is no analogous gap to exploit. One can disagree with Kripke. One cannot use his analogy as a knockdown without noting that its author said it does not work here. The essay says it is “not being eliminative about consciousness”; what it is being is functionalist about the concept, and that is the premise that needed defending.

quote: A mind all of whose parts are systematically locally reliable, relative to their contexts, would be systematically globally reliable. Ergo, a mind that is globally unreliable must contain at least one locally unreliable part. So a causally closed cognitive system inspecting itself for local reliability must discover that at least one step involved in adding the belief of an epiphenomenal inner self is unreliable.
content: The 2013 bracketed edit points the reader to Tiling Agents for Self-Modifying AI (Yudkowsky & Herreshoff, 2013, an unpublished technical report), and that report is a statement of why the requirement in this paragraph cannot be met. The Löbian obstacle it describes is that a consistent agent using a sound proof system cannot prove that the beliefs its own reasoning produces are true, because a system that proves “if I prove P then P” for all P proves P, by Löb’s theorem, and is therefore inconsistent. The “causally closed cognitive system inspecting itself for local reliability” is asked to certify its own parts, which is the thing the theorem forbids in general; what a consistent agent can certify is a strictly weaker system than itself. So the principle “enforce global reliability by enforcing local reliability” is not a design available to any reflectively coherent agent in the essay’s own later formalism, and the “proof of disbelief in zombies” built on it inherits the problem. There is a further difficulty that the essay’s own examples raise: the system that inspects its arithmetic module and finds it locally reliable does so by reasoning that is itself arithmetic, which is Alston’s epistemic circularity again. None of this rescues epiphenomenalism. It does mean that the argument advertised as a knockdown from AI design rests on an agent that cannot exist.

quote: Now that’s what I call a miraculously misleading coincidence—although the word N’Shama arose for completely different reasons, it sounded exactly the right way to make me think it referred to an inner listener.
content: The correction is right (neshamah is from the root for breathing, נשם; hearing is שמע, with an ayin the word lacks), and the essay’s acceptance of it is to its credit. Two things are worth recording. The false etymology was the opening image of a 6,600-word essay and was used there to explain how the “passive listener” intuition arises and to characterize what rabbis believe about the soul; that essay is reprinted in this book without a footnote, so a reader of Zombies! Zombies? alone will still learn that the Hebrew soul is “the hearer.” And the form of the mistake is the one the book most often makes: a fact recalled because it fit the argument, checked by no one before publication, and found wrong by a reader who knew the language. The correction was a day’s work for the commenter and could have been an hour’s for the author. That is the general remedy for most of what these annotations record.
